snippet.title: Monster: Vicky Krieps Reworked the Intimacy to Feel Real | Set Stories
snippet.description:
Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story required Vicky Krieps to find Bridget “Maggie” Sullivan through the smallest details, including what the character would actually wear, read, and do when nobody was watching.

Krieps takes us behind the scenes of Netflix’s Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story to explain how she shaped Bridget’s physicality. During her first costume fitting, she pushed for masculine shoes and questioned clothing choices that would have restricted her movement. For Krieps, those decisions helped distinguish Bridget from the other women around her and gave the character greater physical freedom.

The actor also opens up about developing Bridget’s relationship with Ella Beatty’s Lizzie Borden. She recalls questioning the staging of intimate moments, relying on trust with Beatty, and looking for what was emotionally happening between the two women rather than focusing solely on physical actions.

Krieps also reveals how she used the production’s period furniture and props to immerse herself in Bridget’s world. That attention to the environment even inspired an improvised moment in which Bridget talks to the silverware while alone in the kitchen.

snippet.title: Below: One Accent Had to Make the Family Feel Real | Set Stories
snippet.description:
Josh Hartnett, Mackenzie Davis, and Charlie Heaton had to sound like one believable Newfoundland family for Netflix’s Below — a challenge made more complicated by the many different accents found across the island.

The Below cast joins Collider to discuss immersing themselves in Newfoundland while filming the Netflix series. Because the actors playing the family largely weren't from Newfoundland, they spent time together developing a shared accent and establishing rules that would make it sound like the characters came from the same place. Working alongside local actors, extras, and community members became an important part of that process.

But their Newfoundland immersion went far beyond dialect work. The cast recalls filming near St. John’s and visiting more remote communities, with Hartnett describing the island's landscapes and the extraordinary welcome they received from locals. They even went whale watching and encountered humpback whales during one of their first weekends there.

The actors also learned practical fishing skills for Below, including navigating and driving boats, making fishing nets, gutting fish, rigging, and understanding how fishermen locate promising spots without modern technology. As for mastering fishing knots? That proved a little more difficult.

snippet.title: The Shards: One Costume Silhouette Gave Steven His Walk | Set Stories
snippet.description:
Jordan Roth reveals how fashion, performance art, and a crash course in television acting shaped Steven in FX’s The Shards. From David Bowie and David Sylvian references to a lavender leather jumpsuit, Roth explains how Steven’s distinctive look became inseparable from the character.

In this Collider interview, Roth breaks down working with Ryan Murphy to develop Steven’s aesthetic, including influences from Paris runways, London music culture, and Duran Duran. The actor also shares how costume designers Lou Eyrich, Josh McClenney, and Syreeta Bell helped establish Steven’s silhouette, movement, and unforgettable wardrobe.

Roth also discusses making the transition from theater to television, calling the difference between the two an “extraordinary revelation.” Instead of projecting to the back of a theater, Roth discovered how the camera could capture something as subtle as an eyebrow movement or the smallest change in expression.

Plus, Roth recalls refusing to sit during the first night shoot because of a commitment to keeping Steven’s red pants wrinkle-free, the cast’s off-camera singing and dancing, and bonding over bringing food to set.

snippet.title: Harry Potter: How HBO Is Rebuilding the Wizarding World
snippet.description:
Harry Potter is being rebuilt on an enormous scale for HBO, and some of the biggest challenges have nothing to do with visual effects. The young cast’s education, limited filming windows, practical creatures, Quidditch crowds, and elaborate sets all have to work together.

Behind the scenes at Leavesden Studios, HBO constructed a temporary school for the dozens of young performers working on the series. On particularly large production days, it can accommodate as many as 600 students. While the actors are in class, crews prepare scenes using adult stand-ins so everything is ready when filming can begin.

This Harry Potter behind-the-scenes breakdown also looks at the casting process that selected Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger, and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley after an enormous UK search.

Then there’s Quidditch. Episode 7’s major match required extensive crowd choreography, including roughly seven hours of spectator reaction footage captured during one production day.

From animatronic owls containing around 36,000 individually attached feathers to book-inspired Hogwarts architecture, 1991-era costumes, and returning craftspeople with connections to the original films, HBO is combining a new interpretation with decades of practical Potter filmmaking experience.

snippet.description:
Chris Mundy and Vikash Patel break down how Lanterns grounds its Green Lantern mythology in the rhythms of a buddy-cop drama, drawing inspiration from films like Lethal Weapon, 48 Hrs., Training Day, and Midnight Run.

In this Collider interview, showrunner Chris Mundy and supervising editor and associate producer Vikash Patel explain the creative choices behind the 2026 DC series, including the relationship between Hal Jordan and John Stewart. Mundy reveals that Hal's harsh treatment of John masks more respect, affection, and fear than audiences might initially realize, while Patel discusses how the edit helps reveal those layers.

They also unpack the show's "magical realism" approach: extraordinary things like aliens, holograms, and Green Lantern rings exist alongside interrogations, coffee, tacos, and everyday life without the characters treating them as separate worlds. The pair discuss balancing rapid-fire dialogue with carefully placed pauses, shaping different timelines through performance, and intercutting major Episode 4 sequences to keep multiple stories moving.

Plus, they explain why one extended interrogation became a key showcase for the ring's power and how Lanterns earns its comic-book elements by first establishing a grounded cop-show foundation.

John Francis Daley and Jonathan Goldstein wanted Mayday’s aerial action to feel physically believable, even when visual effects were needed to finish the illusion. The filmmakers explain how real pilots, practical cockpit rigs, footage of French jets over the Mediterranean, and volume technology helped ground Ryan Reynolds’ Cold War adventure.

In this Collider interview, Daley and Goldstein break down the making of Mayday, starring Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh, including an ejection sequence that transitioned to a stunt performer dropping 150 feet down a tree. They also reveal the logistical challenge of shooting the movie’s climactic Moscow parade sequence in Budapest with roughly 1,000 extras, a dozen Soviet tanks, and an ICBM launch vehicle.

The directors also discuss building full-size train cars for an ambitious chase, finding room for Reynolds and Branagh to improvise within their carefully honed script, and why the actors’ contrasting styles made them such an appealing pairing. Plus, they explain the movie’s “ugly beautiful” East Bloc aesthetic and how lessons from Game Night and Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves shaped their approach to balancing comedy, action, scares, and heart.

Animation supervisor Hal Hickel, production visual effects supervisor John Knoll, and property department’s Josh Roth reveal how Jon Favreau’s practical-first philosophy shaped the movie. Knoll discusses designing imagery for an IMAX screen and finding ways to make action visually distinctive, while Roth explains how the prop department searches for vintage objects with the right 1970s aesthetic before transforming them into something that belongs in the Star Wars galaxy.

They also unpack the redesign and animation of Rotta, an unusually athletic Hutt who needed to fight, emote, and form a bond with Grogu.

Pegg explains why learning about the frequency and variety of cyber threats was both “educational and terrifying,” and how coordinated social media activity can be used to create discord and divisiveness.

Brooke digs into another side of the series: the people making enormously consequential decisions while still dealing with their own beliefs, emotions, and relationships. She also discusses stretching herself as a performer, including the challenge of delivering dialogue in Mandarin and Cantonese.

Pegg reveals how Danny becomes more multidimensional in Season 2 as audiences see him away from GCHQ as a father and husband. He also reflects on how quickly technology has caught up with ideas that seemed futuristic when Season 1 was made, including a convincing AI deepfake. Plus, Pegg and Brooke break down difficult technical dialogue, favorite scene partners, and a lengthy sequence that felt like performing a play.

snippet.title: Why Knight of the Seven Kingdoms Threw a Fake Horse Through a Fence
snippet.description:
Director of photography Gustav Danielsson takes Collider behind the scenes of A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, beginning with the seven-on-seven fighting sequence. Rather than building the entire environment with green screen or an LED studio, the production staged the fight on location, using fog and morning mist to help create its gritty atmosphere. VFX was then used to finesse elements such as the smoke and fog.

Danielsson explains how the battle was carefully storyboarded, how a wire-mounted camera created a fast-moving shot over the horses, and how trained horses and a mocap horse were combined to make the action appear dangerous while keeping the animals safe.

The cinematographer also reveals how Ireland’s famously unpredictable conditions affected the shoot. From matching rain and sunshine during Episode 1 to augmenting firelight as natural dusk disappeared, Danielsson explains how the crew worked with changing light rather than against it. He closes by discussing Dunk’s Episode 5 flashback, including the Flea Bottom locations that helped broaden the world of the series.

Despite all that preparation, Sewell says the final step is throwing it away, staying present, and making Hal’s decisions believable to himself, even when the character may be deluding himself.
